```{python}
#| label: setup
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.patches as mpatches
from scipy.optimize import linprog
from _lib.orplot import COLORS
from _lib.toy_network import (WORKERS, JOBS, BIP_EDGES, BIP_POS,
                              bipartite_matching_lp, min_vertex_cover)

card = bipartite_matching_lp()
wtd = bipartite_matching_lp(weighted=True)
cover = min_vertex_cover()

def draw_bip(ax, matching=(), circled=(), labels=None, prices=None):
    for u, v, w in BIP_EDGES:
        p, q = BIP_POS[u], BIP_POS[v]
        hl = (u, v) in matching
        ax.plot([p[0], q[0]], [p[1], q[1]], color=COLORS["weak"] if hl else "#999999",
                lw=3.2 if hl else 1.2, zorder=1)
        if labels:
            t = 0.28 if u in ("Ana", "Dee") else 0.22
            m = (1 - t) * np.array(p) + t * np.array(q)
            ax.text(*m, f"{w}", fontsize=8.5, ha="center", va="center", zorder=3,
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.1", fc="white", ec="none"))
    for v, (x, y) in BIP_POS.items():
        ring = v in circled
        ax.add_patch(mpatches.Circle((x, y), 0.2, fc="#a6d8a8" if ring else "white",
                                     ec="black", lw=2.2 if ring else 1.2, zorder=4))
        ax.text(x, y, v, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, zorder=5)
        if prices is not None:
            ax.text(x + (-0.42 if x < 1 else 0.42), y, f"{prices[v] + 0:g}", ha="center",
                    va="center", fontsize=9.5, color=COLORS["p1"], fontweight="bold")
    ax.set_xlim(-0.65, 2.65); ax.set_ylim(-0.45, 3.45)
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
```

## The idea

Four workers and four jobs; a line means "this worker can do this job." A **matching**
is a set of worker–job pairs in which nobody appears twice. How many workers can be
assigned at once? If each pair has a value, which matching has the largest total value?

In the example, Ana, Ben and Dee can only do $J_1$ or $J_2$, so at most two of them can be
busy, plus Cai: the maximum matching has size $3$. The three green nodes
$\{\text{Cai}, J_1, J_2\}$ prove it: every line touches one of them, and a matching can
use each of them only once.

```{python}
#| label: fig-bipartite
#| fig-cap: "Left: a maximum matching (red) of size 3 in the worker–job graph. The green nodes form a minimum vertex cover: every edge touches one of the three, so no matching can have more than 3 edges. Kőnig's theorem says such a certificate always exists in bipartite graphs. Right: with values on the edges, the best assignment (red) has total value $5 + 6 + 6 = 17$. The blue numbers are dual prices: on every edge, the prices of its two ends add up to at least the edge's value, with equality on the chosen edges, which proves 17 is optimal."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(8.6, 3.8))
draw_bip(axes[0], matching=card["matching"], circled=cover)
axes[0].set_title("maximum matching and minimum cover", fontsize=10)
draw_bip(axes[1], matching=wtd["matching"], labels=True, prices=wtd["price"])
axes[1].set_title("best assignment and dual prices", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

## The math

### Bipartite matching is a flow problem

Add a source $s$ with an arc of capacity 1 to each worker, an arc of capacity 1 from
each job to a sink $t$, and direct every worker–job edge from worker to job. An integer
$s$–$t$ flow is exactly a matching, so by the
[integrality theorem](../shortest-paths-and-flows/max-flow-min-cut.qmd) the maximum
flow is the size of a maximum matching, and augmenting paths find it.

### Kőnig's theorem

A **vertex cover** is a set of nodes touching every edge. Each edge of a matching
needs its own cover node, so every matching is at most as large as every cover.

::: {.callout-important}
## Theorem (Kőnig)
In a bipartite graph, the maximum size of a matching equals the minimum size of a vertex
cover.
:::

Dénes Kőnig published this min-max theorem in 1931, in Hungarian; @schrijver2005 tells
the history. In LP terms it is
[duality](../../linear-programming/duality/lp-duality.qmd) between
$$
\max \sum_e x_e \ \text{ s.t. } \sum_{e \ni v} x_e \le 1 \ (\text{all } v),\ x \ge 0
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\min \sum_v y_v \ \text{ s.t. } y_u + y_v \ge 1 \ (\text{all } uv),\ y \ge 0,
$$
plus the fact that both LPs have integer optima, because the incidence matrix of a
bipartite graph is [totally unimodular](total-unimodularity.qmd).

### The assignment problem and the Hungarian method

With a value $w_{ij}$ on each edge, the **assignment problem** asks for a matching of
maximum total value. Its LP has the same constraints as above, so it is again integral,
and its dual assigns a **price** $p_v$ to every node with $p_i + p_j \ge w_{ij}$ on every
edge. By complementary slackness, a matching is optimal when its edges are **tight**
($p_i + p_j = w_{ij}$) and every unmatched node has price zero.

The **Hungarian method** of @kuhn1955 maintains such prices and searches for a perfect
matching using only tight edges. When the search gets stuck, it adjusts the prices to
make new edges tight, and repeats. Kuhn named it after the Hungarian mathematicians
Kőnig and Egerváry, whose ideas it combines. Its variants run in polynomial time.

### General graphs: odd cycles break integrality

In a non-bipartite graph the matching LP can have **fractional** vertices. In a triangle,
$x_e = \tfrac12$ on all three edges satisfies every degree constraint and has value
$\tfrac32$, but any real matching has only one edge.

```{python}
#| label: fig-odd-cycle
#| fig-cap: "Left: in a triangle, putting 1/2 on every edge satisfies all degree constraints ($x$-values at each node add to 1) and gives the matching LP the value 3/2, although a matching can contain only one edge. Right: Edmonds' odd-set inequality for the three nodes says the edges inside them can carry at most $(3-1)/2 = 1$ in total; it cuts off the fractional point and leaves only real matchings."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(7.4, 3.0))
tri = {"u": (0, 0), "v": (2, 0), "w": (1, 1.6)}
E = [("u", "v"), ("v", "w"), ("w", "u")]
for ax, frac in zip(axes, (True, False)):
    for (a, b_) in E:
        p, q = np.array(tri[a]), np.array(tri[b_])
        hl = frac or (a, b_) == ("u", "v")
        ax.plot(*np.array([p, q]).T, color=COLORS["weak"] if hl else "#999999",
                lw=3 if hl else 1.2, ls="--" if frac else "-", zorder=1)
        if frac:
            m = (p + q) / 2
            ax.text(*m, "1/2", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=10,
                    bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.15", fc="white", ec="none"), zorder=3)
    for v, (x, y) in tri.items():
        ax.add_patch(mpatches.Circle((x, y), 0.17, fc="white", ec="black", lw=1.2, zorder=4))
        ax.text(x, y, v, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=10, zorder=5)
    ax.set_xlim(-0.4, 2.4); ax.set_ylim(-0.4, 2.0); ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
axes[0].set_title("matching LP: value 3/2", fontsize=10)
axes[1].set_title("with $x_{uv} + x_{vw} + x_{wu} \\leq 1$: value 1", fontsize=10)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

@edmonds1965b found the missing constraints. For every set $U$ of nodes with an **odd**
number of elements,
$$
\sum_{e \subseteq U} x_e \;\le\; \frac{|U| - 1}{2},
$$
since a matching can pair up at most $(|U| - 1)/2$ couples inside $U$.

::: {.callout-important}
## Theorem (Edmonds' matching polytope)
For any graph, the degree constraints $\sum_{e \ni v} x_e \le 1$, the bounds $x \ge 0$,
and the odd-set inequalities together describe the convex hull of all matchings: every
vertex of this polytope is a matching.
:::

There are exponentially many odd sets, so this LP cannot be written out in full.
Instead, the **blossom algorithm** of @edmonds1965a finds a maximum matching directly in
polynomial time, by finding augmenting paths and shrinking odd cycles ("blossoms") when
they get in the way. In the same paper Edmonds argued that "efficient" should mean
"polynomial-time," an idea that later became central to complexity theory.

## Why it works

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Proof sketch: Kőnig's theorem
Weak duality gives "every matching $\le$ every cover." For equality, both LPs above have
the bipartite incidence matrix (or its transpose) as their constraint matrix, which is
totally unimodular. So the primal has an integer optimal solution, which is a 0/1 vector
(the degree constraints keep each $x_e \le 1$): a matching. The dual has an integer
optimal solution, which can be taken 0/1: a vertex cover. By strong duality their sizes
are equal.
:::

## In practice

- **Assignment problems** (people to shifts, tasks to machines, students to projects)
  with one-to-one constraints are solved exactly by LP or by Hungarian-type algorithms,
  even with thousands of items.
- **Once extra rules appear** (skills, time windows, a worker doing several tasks with a
  budget), integrality is usually lost and the problem becomes an integer program. The
  matching structure then often provides a strong relaxation.
- **Edmonds' theorem is the model** for polyhedral combinatorics: describe the convex hull
  of the solutions, and LP duality gives min-max theorems and algorithms. Cutting-plane
  methods for hard problems try to imitate it.
